content.title: Discussion of and comparison with variational dropout missing. Otherwise good contribution
content.review:
Summary: The authors propose a sparse training algorithm where the mask is encoded as a Bernoulli variable trained through reparameterization and Gumbel softmax. The network is initialized densely and gradually pruned until the desired sparsity is reached. The work's main goal is to have a sparsity algorithm that performs specifications globally rather than layer-wise.

Strong points:
The work is technically sound, easy to read, and understand. Since sparsification during training is still under-explored, this is a very valuable contribution.

Weak points:
- A weak point is the technically unsound categorization of the algorithm. The authors state that their algorithm "train[s] sparse neural networks from scratch," but Algorithm 1 indicates that the network is initialized densely and sparsified over time. As such, the presented algorithm is not a "sparse training" algorithm per se but more akin to compression algorithms, which start with a dense network. I view the work most similar to Kusupati et al., 2020 and Molchanov et al. 2017 (citation missing).
- Molchanov et al., 2017 is the most similar work in that they start from a dense network and sparsity the network via the reparameterization trick of a binary variable over time. In fact, variational dropout is characterized by the very same parameterization that was introduced by the authors. The only difference is the global parameter capacity constraint.
- Discussion of related work is incomplete or inaccurate. The related work discusses Wortsman et al. 2019 and Kusupati et al. as sparse training algorithms, but these start with dense weights or have gradient updates for all weights, and such do not constitute sparse training algorithms. A citation of Dettmers & Zettlemoyer, 2019, is missing. A discussion between the difference of sparse training and sparsification from dense weights is missing. Since the former problem is much more difficult it is an important distinction.
- Table 1 shows results on CIFAR-10 but only compares to two methods and is thus not very comprehensive. It is unclear why these two methods were chosen. A comparison with variational dropout is missing.
- Table 3: There is a handful of other methods compared at 10% of weights on ImageNet, and a comparison between the author's method and other methods is missing on this level. A comparison with variational dropout is missing. A comparison with variational dropout would show how beneficial it is to constraint the number of parameters during optimizations rather than after training and would be a great contribution. This is particularly critical in these experiments since variational dropout is quite stable at very high sparsity values. 


Recommendation (short):
In its current form, I recommend rejecting this work. The main reason is that the method is very similar to variational dropout, which is not cited or discussed. From the experiments, it is unclear what advantage a capacity constrain has over variational dropout where the constraint is applied after training.

Recommendation (long):
The main point for rejection is similarity and failure to discuss and compare against variational dropout. Beyond that, the classification of the algorithm and discussion of related work is a bit sloppy: There is a clear difference between sparse training and network compression. This work is closer to network compression than sparse training. Blurring the line between these two areas makes working in either subfield confusing for both authors and readers. I would not like to see a paper accepted that fuels that confusion.

Comments for authors:
Thank you for your contributions. I think this is good work, but it needs a bit more polishing. I see the comparison with variational dropout as critical to making your work solid. Beyond this, I only see minor details that need to be reworked. If you decide to do the variational dropout experiments, I do not require your algorithm to be better or more favorable. If you can show that your global constraint during optimization has an advantage, that is great, but it is equally interesting if it has no advantage. If you include these experiments and fix the issues above, I am happy to accept your work for publication. Here some further comments and questions to improve your draft:
- Why did you choose the exact methods to compare against in Table 1?
- Table 1 is difficult to read. I know it isn't easy to improve it for sparse network papers since there are so many variables to display. Can you come up with something more readable?
- Can you say something about the variance of weights across layers with you re-run your algorithm with different seeds. Is it always like in Figure 2?
- Why did you choose those particular methods to compare to in Table 3? Why those sparsity ratios? There are a lot of methods that compare at 10% and 20% weights. It might be useful to include these data to give a complete picture.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Q1. Technically unsound categorization of the algorithm.

A1. Thanks for your reminding. Actually, there are no explicit definitions for these categories. We think  two proper ways could be to divide them according to 1) whether the method is applied after or during training; 2) whether the network is changing from sparse to sparse or dense to sparse.  We will address this issue in the later version.

Q2. Molchanov et al., 2017 is the most similar work in that they start from a dense network and sparsity the network via the reparameterization trick of a binary variable over time. In fact, it is characterized by the very same parameterization that was introduced by the authors. The only difference is the global parameter capacity constraint.

A2. This is a misunderstanding. Of course, the high level idea of reparameterizing with respect to probability is not novel. The challenging lies in how to work on the probability space directly, which is one of the main contribution of our paper. Most all of the existing methods including Molchanov et al., 2017 need to reparameterize further (e.g., using hard sigmoid, hard concrete) to evade some challengings (e.g., optimizing on the probability space directly). Such further parameterization tricks can cause the problems such as 1)gradient vanishing (e.g., induced by KL divergenence function pattern in Molchanov et al., 2017); 2) the probabilities cannot converge to 0 and 1 after training, leading to noticeable gaps in training and testing time and the testing time performance also shows considerable variances among different runs (e.g., simply make a cut-off to obtain testing time model rather than sampling in in Molchanov et al.). These limitations can be found in the experiments results of [1], Molchanov et al., 2017. By the way, Molchanov et al. is not based on the reparameterization trick of a binary variable but based on a Gaussian random variable, which makes a distinction to ours. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to directly work on the probability space and with the global sparsity constraint the random mask can finally converge to a deterministic one during training. In the later version, we will include the comparison experimental results to show the superiority of our method.

Q3. Table 1 shows results on CIFAR-10 but only compares to two methods and is thus not very comprehensive. It is unclear why these two methods were chosen.

A3. We notice that CIFAR-10 is not challenging enough to evaluate the performance of  pruning methods. We compare our method with two classical methods on CIFAR-10 to show some  appealing properties of our method. PBW (Pruning by Weight, Han et al. (2015a))  is a classic weight pruning method widely used and MLPrune is an effective pruning method based on Hessian, showing superior performance against classic Hessian based methods (OBD). Besides, MLPrune shows superior performances against three dynamic sparse training methods (SET, DEEPR, DSR) on CIFAR experiments [2]. We compare with these three dynamic sparse training methods implicitly.

Q4. There is a handful of other methods compared at 10\% of weights on ImageNet. A comparison between the author's method and other methods is missing on this level in Table 3.

A4. We notice that the size of compressed ResNet50 at the level of 10\% is comparable with MobileNet and existing pruning methods cannot achieve significantly better performance than that of MobileNet. Therefore, in real applications, we can choose the MobileNet other than compressing ResNet50 at the level of 10\%. In the later version, we will include the results at 10\%.

Q5. Can you say something about the variance of weights across layers with you re-run your algorithm with different seeds. Is it always like in Figure 2?

A5. Actually, our method is very stable. We will report the performances of our method with different seeds.

[1] The State of Sparsity in Deep Neural Networks

[2] Picking Winning Tickets Before Training by Preserving Gradient Flow

content.title: initial review
content.review:
The paper proposes to jointly learn differentiable masks with model parameters, so as to train sparse neural networks from scratch. The paper tackles the difficulty of identifying feasible layer-wise sparsity ratios through a global sparsity constraint.

### pros
* the paper conducts extensive experiments for VGG19 and ResNet32 on CIFAR-10/100, and ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1k.
* the paper provides the ablation study to visualize the layerwise sparsity after using the probmask.

### cons
1. The idea of jointly learning differentiable masks with model parameters (and with the Gumbel trick) is not novel; it is better to cite the existing works, e.g. [1, 2, 3]. Without making a clear distinguishment/comparison, it is hard to identify the contribution of the paper.
2. The related work section 2.1 should include more recent works (i.e. after the year 2018). Besides, even though the methods from the category of the 'sparse training from scratch' are the main competitors of the proposed method, it is still better to compare with other recent progress (e.g. pruning after the training [4, 5]).
3. The existing results evaluate the accuracy in terms of the same pruning rate; however, due to the different layerwise sparsity ratios, right now it is hard to evaluate the performance of different methods in a more realistic setup (e.g. similar FLOPs).
4. In ImageNet results, some results are taken from the prior work while the others are trained by authors; due to the potential different implementation details of the dense baseline, the current comparison may not be meaningful and it is suggested to also include the quality drop score compared to the dense baseline (corresponding to the same experimental setup/paper). 
5. The ablation study w.r.t. the hyper-parameter tuning overhead should be provided, as the current one introduces both Adam and SGD optimizer, with different learning rates, and with a cosine learning rate schedule (different from the conventional stage-wise learning rate schedule).  It is worth to check the sensitivity of these hyper-parameters. It is also unclear to me if the other competitors are using the same learning rate schedule or have the same amount of hyper-parameter tuning or not; based on the ImageNet description in the appendix, a list of non-standard hyper-parameters are being used, while some of the results are from the existing papers.
6. As the paper proposes to jointly learn masks and weights, it will double the total number of trainable parameters. Thus, a study in terms of the computation overhead should be included.

### reference
1. Operation-aware soft channel pruning using differentiable masks, ICML 2020.
2. Structured Pruning of Large Language Models, 2019.
3. Learning Sparse Neural Networks through $L_0$ Regularization, ICLR 2018
4. Comparing Rewinding and Fine-tuning in Neural Network Pruning, ICLR 2020.
5. Good Subnetworks Provably Exist: Pruning via Greedy Forward Selection, ICML 2020

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
First of all thank you very much for your hard work on reviewing and helpful suggestions.

1.We will cite the mentioned works in the newer version. [1] concentrates on solving the problem of Network Slimming in channel pruning, a different area from us. [3] is discussed in the original version of paper and is placed in the appendix due to space limit. [2] follows the practice of [3] and applys it into structured pruning of language models. 

The high level idea of reparameterizing with respect to probability is not novel but the challenge lies in how to work on the probability space directly, which is one of the main contribution of our paper. All of the existing methods including Srinivas et al. 2017, Louizos et al. 2017. need to reparameterize further (e.g., using hard sigmoid, hard concrete) to evade some challenges (e.g., optimizing on the probability space directly). Such further parameterization tricks can cause the problems such as 1)gradient vanishing 2) the probabilities cannot converge to 0 and 1 after training, leading to noticeable gaps in training and testing time and the testing time performance also shows considerable variances among different runs. These limitations can be found in Srinivas et al. 2017, Louizos et al. 2017, Molchanov  et al., 2017 and experiments results of [1]. Louizos et al. 2017 even fails to work on ImageNet due to the second problem. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to directly work on the probability space and with the global sparsity constraint the random mask can finally converge to a deterministic one during training. We avoid such gradient vanishing and discrepancy between training and testing problem, and finally achieve SOTA results on large scale and high pruning rate settings.

2.Thanks for your information. We will cite the mentioned works in the newer version. [5] is a work focusing on channel pruning, so it is not compared with ProbMask. The training scheme of [4] needs iterative training and rewinding, and therefore the training epoch is much longer than us. So [4] is not compared with us.

3.Thanks for your suggestion. The sparsity indicates the final model size. Model size is also an important metric in deployments. We will include FLOPS in the newer version.

4.We will consider adding the accuracy drop in the new version.

5.We have stated in the paper that the parameter setting in the ImageNet experiments is the same with that used in STR(the third line in 4.3). Actually cosine schedule is also widely used these days and have quite steady performance. You may check this file [8] and compare with our setting. The only parameter needed for tuning is the learning rate for Adam optimizer and this is obtained via CIFAR-10 experiments on Conv4 and applied directly to other networks and datasets. Other parameters like batch size, weight decay, learning rate for weights are set the same with others' settings (STR, [6], [7]).

6.Although the trainable parameter number is doubled, the computational cost is just added a little. The gradient to probability can be obtained directly by the gradient to the sparse weights ($w\circ m$). There is no matrix multiplication involved in the calculation of gradient of probability form the gradient to sparse weights. The computation overhead is $O(n)$, and it doesn't add much to the $O(n^{3})$ ($O(n^{2.3}$ if optimized)) for matrix multiplication. 

[1] Operation-aware soft channel pruning using differentiable masks, ICML 2020.
[2] Structured Pruning of Large Language Models, 2019.
[3] Learning Sparse Neural Networks through L_0 Regularization, ICLR 2018
[4] Comparing Rewinding and Fine-tuning in Neural Network Pruning, ICLR 2020.
[5] Good Subnetworks Provably Exist: Pruning via Greedy Forward Selection, ICML 2020
[6] Rethinking the value of network pruning
[7] What’s hidden in a randomly weighted neural network?
[8] https://github.com/RAIVNLab/STR/blob/master/configs/largescale/resnet50-dense.yaml

display_title: Elegant and effective method for sparse training, but very similar to AutoPrune

content.title: Elegant and effective method for sparse training, but very similar to AutoPrune
content.review:
This paper proposes an elegant solution for training a sparse network from scratch, i.e. identifying an unstructured mask to prune the weights at the same time as learning the weights. The method introduces masking probabilities for each individual weight, which are trained with gumbel trick to make the problem differentiable. The global sparsity is then easily controlled by the sum of probabilities. This leads to a very elegant and easy to understand (and implement) formulation. The method is compared against SOTA sparse training methods - especially Soft Threshold Weight Reparametrization (STR) method, and is shown to beat it in terms of final accuracy for given sparsity targets.

The trouble I have with this paper is that it is extremely similar to another paper that is not cited: "AutoPrune: Automatic Network Pruning by Regularizing Auxiliary Parameters" by Xiao et al - NeurIPS 2018. This paper essentially has the same solution, but in logit space rather than probability space - meaning that instead of using probabilities s_i directly, it uses sigmoid(h_i). The paper uses straight though estimator to update the h_i variables instead of using the gumbel trick, and controls the global sparsity in exactly the same way as proposed here. It is a *very* similar method, so I think this paper must cite AutoPrune and also compare itself against it and discuss the differences.

I like this paper, and I think the results are significant, but the biggest issue is the similarity of it to AutoPrune. It's not clear to me whether this method is better than AutoPrune in any way - and if it is, why. Unfortunately a proper quantitative comparison may require reimplementation of that work, but it may be very easy to do given the similarity of the two works. But until there is a satisfactory discussion / comparison with AutoPrune, I think this paper shouldn't be accepted.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
Thanks for your hard work on reviewing and constructive comments. Maybe there are some misunderstandings on the differences between AutoPrune and ProbMask.

1.Autoprune is not reparameterized respect to probability but to auxiliary parameters. It cannot explicitly control sparsity. Besides, the absolute value of importance measure h(m) is not globally comparable across layers. Essentially it needs to choose proper sparsity budget for different layers. Autoprune is more of the way of DNW(Discovering neural wirings). DNW also assigns a score to the corresponding weights and outputs the mask by ranking the weights. This will cause performance collapse at high pruning rate. Such phenomenon has already been observed at DNW at the ImageNet experiments at 98\% pruning rates. Besides there is gap in training and testing time because h(m) of pruned weights will not necessarily converge to zero.

2.Autoprune actually don't use straight-through estimator and more importantly as clarified above, our work have a big distinction with theirs. Besides, Autoprune has gradient vanishing problem when use softplus function. 

3.The sparsity of Autoprune is controlled by a regularization term, not the same form of us. Users of Autoprune have to search for regularization parammeters to achieve a desired model size. This sometimes takes 2 to 3 times to run the algorithm with different parameters.

4.Autoprune only demonstrates the results on ImageNet for ResNet50 for sparsity around 55\%. with 0.4\% accuracy drop. This result is too weak and can be easily achieved just by basic weight pruning(PBW, Han et al., 2015b, [1]). Accuracy drop of PBW is just 0.06\% at 60\% sparsity, even better than AutoPrune. PBW falls behind ProbMask in high pruning rate. It can be expected that Autoprune is not a strong competitor against us, especially under high pruning rates.

All in all, AutoPrune is in another category that may be named as deterministic method, not in the category of probabilistic method. The performance gap between AutoPrune and ProbMask can be expected from the gap between Autoprune and PBW and the gap between PBW and ProbMask. 

[1] Rethinking the value of network pruning

display_title: The paper if fine, but it lacks a bit of rigor and novelty

content.title: The paper if fine, but it lacks a bit of rigor and novelty
content.review:
### Summary:

The paper formulates the training of sparse neural networks as an optimization with respect to weights and weight mask parameters. Constraining the optimization by an upper bound on the number of connections is a complex problem, and the authors suggest a relaxation of this optimization problem where the mask parameters are replaced by the probability of masking the parameter.

This relaxation makes it possible to simplify the constraint on the $L_0$ norm of $w$, to a linear constraint on the probability $s$. The authors finally apply a projected gradient algorithm on this loss function: they use the gumbel softmax trick to derive differentiable gradients through the relationship between s and m, and derive rigorously the projection operator adapted to the constraint on $s$.

The authors apply their methods on CIFAR 10, CIFAR 100 and ImageNet with large VGG and ResNet architectures. They achieve better results than contemporary methods for 99% and 99.5% sparsity level. Out of the few analyses the more interesting in my opinion is to show that the probability converges empirically to a sparse binary distribution with an appropriate annealing schedule on gumbel softmax temperature.

### Critical review:

The mathematical formulation in section 3 is not ideal and it seems to lack rigor. How is the equation (1) compatible with the definition $ K = k || m ||_0$ given inline afterwards ?

I think it is misleading to call (2) a "reformulation" of problem (1) and it should be called a "relaxation" or something like that since the two problems are not equivalent: the constraint is softer in (2) since it applies on the probability only.

After the intro it sounds like the method is training sparse networks throughout the training. But according to compute equation (4) and (5) the gumbel softmax gradient need the computation where m = sigmoid (...), and the mask takes values strictly in ]0,1[, therefore, the training seems to be performed with a dense network, and only at test time the network is made sparse. This should be stated clearly somewhere.

Regarding the novelty, the essential mathematical innovations do not seem particularly novel: the relaxation from (1) to (2) is similar to the one in Srinivas et al. 2017 and something similar to this gumbel softmax trick was used in that Louizos et al. 2017.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
Thanks for your hard work on reviewing and constructive comments.

1."Achieve better results than contemporary methods for 99\% and 99.5\% sparsity level." Actually, ProbMask achieve SOTA results on 90\% to 99\% sparsity. In ImageNet experiments, the gap from ProbMask to STOA STR achieves 1.1\% at 95\%, 5.37\% at 98\%, 10.72\% at 99\%. The gap is huge considering today's demand for accuracy and low-resource applications.

2.Sorry about the typo, it is should be $K=kn$. Thanks for your correction. We will fix it in the later version.

3.Thanks for your correction. Strictly speaking, (2) is a relaxation from (1). We deem the problem as reformulation because empirical observations show that probabilities converge to 0 or 1 after training. But your suggestion is great and we will update it later to avoid confusion.

4.Thanks for your suggestion. We will state it clearly in the paper. 

5.The high level idea of reparameterizing with respect to probability is not novel but the challenge lies in how to work on the probability space directly, which is one of the main contribution of our paper. Most of the existing methods including Srinivas et al. 2017, Louizos et al. 2017. need to reparameterize further (e.g., using hard sigmoid, hard concrete) to evade some challengings (e.g., optimizing on the probability space directly). Such further parameterization tricks can cause the problems such as 1)gradient vanishing 2) the probabilities cannot converge to 0 and 1 after training, leading to noticeable gaps in training and testing time and the testing time performance also shows considerable variances among different runs. These limitations can be found in Srinivas et al. 2017, Louizos et al. 2017 and experiments results of [1]. Louizos et al. 2017 even fails to work on ImageNet due to the second problem. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to directly work on the probability space and with the global sparsity constraint the random mask can finally converge to a deterministic one during training. We avoid such gradient vanishing and discrepancy between training and testing problem, and finally achieve SOTA results on large scale and high pruning rate settings.
